title: Nature and Purpose of Business
tagline: What makes an activity a business, the objectives it pursues, and the economic role it plays. Unit weight: 10 marks.

overview.intro: Commerce begins with a deceptively simple question: what counts as business? A hobby that sells a few items is not a business, while a large factory that loses money still is. The difference lies in intention, continuity and the organised production or exchange of goods and services for value. This unit defines business and its characteristics, separates commerce from industry and trade, sets out the economic, social and human objectives an enterprise pursues, and explains the role business plays in an economy by converting resources into the goods and services people need.

facts.label: Definition
facts.value: An economic activity organised to produce, buy or sell goods and services regularly in order to earn profit.

facts.label: Commerce scope
facts.value: Industry, trade and the auxiliaries of trade (transport, banking, insurance, warehousing, advertising).

facts.label: Objectives
facts.value: Economic (profit and growth), social (service to society), human (satisfaction and development of people).

facts.label: Unit weight
facts.value: 10 marks of the 80-mark Theory paper in the registered 2027 Commerce syllabus.

learningOutcomes: Define business and state its essential characteristics.
Distinguish business from industry, trade and commerce.
Classify business objectives as economic, social and human.
Explain the role of business in an economy.
Identify the auxiliaries of trade that support business.

blocks.text: Business is an economic activity that involves the production, purchase or sale of goods and services on a regular basis with the object of earning profit. The word regular matters: a one-off sale of an old bicycle is not business, while a shop that opens every day selling the same bicycle is. Business also involves risk, because the outcome of every venture depends on conditions the firm cannot control, and it implies dealing with other people, since nothing is produced or sold without customers, suppliers, workers or lenders.

items.meaning: Organised economic activity carried on regularly for profit through production, purchase or sale.
The stage that converts raw material into finished or semi-finished goods.
The actual exchange of goods and services, the final step in the chain.
The whole of exchange including industry, trade and the auxiliaries that make trade possible.
The reward for bearing risk and the means of surviving and growing.

blocks.caption: Characteristics of business and what each implies
rows: Deals in goods and services for value, not as a hobby or a service without consideration
Creates utility or moves it to where it is wanted
Same activity repeated, so systems, records and reputation develop
Income must exceed cost or the venture cannot continue
Uncertainty of demand, cost and competition must be managed
Customers, suppliers, employees and lenders all shape decisions

items.text: A person who knits one sweater and sells it for pocket money.
items.note: No business: the activity is neither regular nor organised for profit.

items.text: A knitter who supplies a shop every month with a fixed range.
items.note: Business: regularity, exchange and the profit motive are all present.

blocks.text: Commerce is the wider term. It covers everything that bridges the gap between the maker and the user of a product: industry, which creates form utility by changing raw material; trade, which creates possession or place utility by transferring ownership; and the auxiliaries of trade, which make that transfer physically and financially possible. The auxiliaries are transport, banking, insurance, warehousing and advertising, and a business cannot function without at least several of them even if it never exports.

blocks.caption: Commerce, industry and trade distinguished
rows: Support and finance the movement of goods

items: Primary industry works with nature: agriculture, fishing, mining.
Secondary industry converts: manufacturing and construction.
Tertiary industry provides services: transport, banking, insurance.
Commerce includes all three wherever they support exchange.
Direct trade is between producer and consumer; indirect trade adds a middleman.

blocks.text: The chain is worth memorising as a sequence: raw material passes through industry to become a finished good, auxiliaries carry and finance it while it waits, and trade finally passes it to the person who will use it. A failure at any link stops the chain, which is why a factory can be productive yet fail if transport or credit collapses.

learn.title: Objectives of business: economic, social and human

blocks.text: Objectives give direction, and a firm without them cannot measure anything. Economic objectives concern survival and growth: earning adequate profit, creating demand for its products, and expanding so that it can serve more people. Social objectives concern the obligation of business to the society that permits it to exist: supplying quality goods at fair prices, avoiding exploitation, protecting the environment and contributing to the community. Human objectives concern the people inside the firm: fair remuneration, working conditions, participation, and the development of skill and personality.

blocks.caption: Economic, social and human objectives
rows: Survival, adequate profit, growth and market standing
Profit, sales, return on capital, market share
Quality at fair price, no exploitation, environmental care, community contribution
Fair wages, working conditions, participation, training, dignity
Turnover, satisfaction surveys, training hours, injury rates

blocks.text: The three categories can conflict, and the art of management lies in holding them together. Cutting wages raises profit and damages the human objective; refusing to sell to a segment that cannot pay protects the social objective and reduces revenue. The healthiest firms treat the social and human objectives as constraints within which the economic objective must be achieved, rather than as optional extras to be abandoned when margins are thin.

items.text: A textile firm installing effluent treatment despite the cost.
items.note: The social objective constrains the economic one, and the cost is accepted as the price of licence to operate.

items.text: A firm running a training academy for its machine operators.
items.note: The human objective also serves the economic one, because skilled operators produce fewer defects.

learn.title: The role of business in an economy

blocks.text: Business converts scattered resources into goods and services that people want, and in doing so performs several functions for the economy as a whole. It produces goods that satisfy wants, generates employment for people with different skills, creates national income which is the base of tax revenue, and encourages innovation as firms compete for customers. It also facilitates the circulation of money, raises the standard of living through wider availability, and supports regional development when industry is located away from the largest cities.

items: Production of goods and services converts resources into wanted utility.
Employment generation gives households income and the economy demand.
Wealth creation and tax revenue fund public services.
Innovation and competition improve quality and lower prices over time.
Distribution through trade moves goods to where they are valued most.
Risk bearing by entrepreneurs absorbs shocks that would otherwise fall on households.

blocks.caption: Auxiliaries of trade and the gap each fills
rows: Goods are made in one place and wanted in another
Payments and credit are needed between distant parties
Risk of loss in transit or storage must be borne somewhere
Goods are produced continuously but bought seasonally
Buyers cannot want what they do not know exists

items.text: A rice mill in one state supplying shops in three others.
items.note: Transport, warehousing and banking together complete what production alone cannot.

items.text: A trader insures a consignment before it travels by road.
items.note: Insurance shifts the risk so that neither the maker nor the buyer carries the full exposure.

keyPoints: Business is an economic activity carried on regularly through production, purchase or sale for profit.
Regularity, profit motive, risk and dealing with others distinguish business from a casual sale.
Commerce covers industry, trade and the auxiliaries of trade.
Industry creates form utility; trade creates possession and place utility.
The auxiliaries are transport, banking, insurance, warehousing and advertising.
Economic objectives are survival, profit and growth.
Social objectives are fair price, quality, environmental care and community contribution.
Human objectives are fair wages, conditions, participation and development of people.
Business generates employment, national income and innovation in an economy.
The three objective categories must be balanced, not traded off one against another.
examFocus: Definition questions want the definition plus four characteristics, each explained in a line.
Objectives questions are marked on the three-way classification, so state the category before listing.
Commerce questions should name the specific auxiliary that solves the specific gap.

vocabulary.meaning: Organised economic activity carried on regularly for the production or exchange of goods and services for profit.
Whole of exchange including industry, trade and the auxiliaries that support them.
Stage of production that converts raw material into finished or semi-finished goods.
Actual buying and selling of goods and services.
Services such as transport, banking, insurance, warehousing and advertising that assist trade.
Power of a good to satisfy a want, created as form, place, possession or time utility.
Excess of revenue over cost, the reward for risk and the source of continuity.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a characteristic of business?
questions.explanation: Every business carries risk from demand, cost and competition, so absence of risk would disqualify an activity from being a business.

questions.prompt: A furniture maker converts timber into tables. This creates:
questions.explanation: Converting raw material into a finished product changes its form, which is the utility created by industry.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an auxiliary of trade?
questions.explanation: Warehousing bridges the time gap between continuous production and seasonal demand, supporting trade rather than producing goods itself.

questions.prompt: A company that pays low wages to raise dividends while ignoring safety standards is failing mainly on:
questions.explanation: Wages and working conditions belong to the human objective, and safety and community welfare to the social one, so both are being traded away for profit.

questions.prompt: The branch of business that converts raw material into finished goods, creating form utility, is called __________ .
questions.explanation: Industry is the production stage of the chain, lying before trade and supported by the auxiliaries of trade.

questions.prompt: The set of services that bridge the gaps between production and consumption, such as transport, banking and insurance, is described as the auxiliaries of __________ .
questions.explanation: These services do not produce or sell goods themselves, but without them trade could not reach the final consumer.

questions.answer: Four characteristics are: it is an economic activity dealing in goods and services for value; it is carried on regularly rather than as a one-off transaction; it aims at profit, which is the reward for bearing risk; and it involves risk and dealing with other people such as customers, suppliers and employees. Production or exchange of goods is also expected.
questions.explanation: Each characteristic needs a line showing what it means in practice, since a bare list earns only partial credit.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between economic and social objectives of business with examples.
questions.answer: Economic objectives are those the firm pursues for itself and its owners: survival, adequate profit, growth and market standing, judged by profit, sales and market share. Social objectives are those it owes to the society that allows it to operate: supplying quality goods at fair prices, avoiding exploitation, protecting the environment and contributing to the community, judged by compliance, audits and community investment. A firm installing effluent treatment is meeting a social objective, while the same firm opening a new branch is meeting an economic one.
questions.explanation: The distinction must be drawn on who benefits, and each side needs its own example.

questions.prompt: Explain the auxiliaries of trade and the gap each one fills.
questions.answer: Transport closes the gap between where goods are produced and where they are wanted by creating place utility. Warehousing closes the gap between continuous production and seasonal or uneven demand by creating time utility. Banking closes the gap between distant parties who must pay and be paid, and by supplying credit for the period between production and sale. Insurance closes the gap created by risk, since the possibility of loss in transit, fire or theft must be borne by someone and a premium transfers it to a specialist. Advertising closes the information gap, because a buyer cannot demand a product of whose existence she is unaware. Together these auxiliaries allow a manufacturer to reach a consumer in another region without ever meeting her.
questions.explanation: Full marks need each auxiliary paired with the specific gap it fills, not merely a list of five services.

questions.prompt: A food-processing company has doubled its profit by cutting quality checks and paying workers by output alone. Worker injuries have risen and two contamination complaints were received. Classify the objectives affected and recommend a course of action.
questions.answer: The company is meeting its economic objectives: profit has doubled. It is breaching its social objective on quality and safety, since contamination complaints show the product it supplies is not of the standard society is entitled to expect, and it is breaching its human objective by paying purely on output, which rewards speed over care and directly encourages the injuries. In the long run the two failures feed back into the economic objective through recalls, litigation, penalties and staff turnover, so the profit is not sustainable. The course of action is to restore quality checks as a non-negotiable standard, introduce a safety component into the pay formula alongside output, and report both changes to the board with the incident data. The three objectives must be held together, because a social or human breach eventually appears as an economic loss.
questions.explanation: Marks depend on classifying each failure correctly, showing the feedback into profit, and recommending action that restores the balance rather than simply apologising.
